official_sources.title: NIST uncertainty components and error distinction
official_sources.authority: National Institute of Standards and Technology
official_sources.finding: NIST separates Type A components evaluated statistically from Type B components evaluated by other means and warns that measurement error and measurement uncertainty are different concepts.
official_sources.limitation: Classification alone does not assign numerical values; each component still needs a documented distribution, standard uncertainty and evidence.

official_sources.title: NIST combined standard uncertainty
official_sources.authority: National Institute of Standards and Technology
official_sources.finding: NIST defines combined standard uncertainty as the estimated standard deviation of the result and combines component standard uncertainties using the law of propagation, including covariances where appropriate.
official_sources.limitation: Root-sum-of-squares is invalid when correlation is ignored or components are not expressed as standard uncertainties.

official_sources.title: NIST law of propagation of uncertainty
official_sources.authority: National Institute of Standards and Technology
official_sources.finding: NIST gives the propagation law using sensitivity coefficients, component variances and covariance terms for a measurement model.
official_sources.limitation: The linearized propagation model must be checked for adequacy when clipping, extrema selection or other nonlinear steps dominate.

official_sources.title: NIST expanded uncertainty and coverage factor
official_sources.authority: National Institute of Standards and Technology
official_sources.finding: NIST defines expanded uncertainty U as a coverage factor k multiplied by combined standard uncertainty and states that the chosen k and associated confidence interpretation must be reported.
official_sources.limitation: Using k=2 does not automatically prove exact 95 percent coverage when normality, degrees of freedom or reliability assumptions do not hold.

official_sources.title: NIST uncertainty reporting requirements
official_sources.authority: National Institute of Standards and Technology
official_sources.finding: NIST requires reports to identify uncertainty components, their evaluation methods, the combined or expanded uncertainty, coverage factor and enough information to reproduce the result.
official_sources.limitation: A well-formed statement is not evidence that the underlying raster, datum or geometry is correct.

official_sources.title: JCGM uncertainty of a difference with correlation
official_sources.authority: Joint Committee for Guides in Metrology / BIPM
official_sources.finding: JCGM states that correlation affects the standard uncertainty of a difference: uncorrelated inputs combine by root-sum-of-squares, positive covariance lowers the difference uncertainty, and negative covariance raises it.
official_sources.limitation: The covariance between parcel minimum and maximum cells cannot be assumed from spatial proximity; it must be estimated or bounded.

official_sources.title: USGS lidar and DEM absolute vertical accuracy validation
official_sources.finding: USGS requires verification and reporting of absolute and relative vertical accuracy and separately assesses NVA and VVA for both point data and derived DEMs.
official_sources.limitation: Project-level accuracy statistics do not directly certify the uncertainty of a specific parcel extrema pair.

official_sources.title: USGS lidar accuracy equations and quality-level thresholds
official_sources.finding: USGS defines vertical RMSE from checkpoint differences, defines RMSEv to include survey error, and distinguishes absolute accuracy from relative or internal precision.
official_sources.limitation: RMSE is not a deterministic bound, and older 95-percent multipliers must not be applied when the governing current standard uses a different reporting convention.
